method: COMPILED FROM 3 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media' (last updated June 2021), 29 claims; LICENCE: © The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne; Terms clause 5.2, personal use only; paraphrased and hash-anchored (read at the RCH website Terms and Conditions, clause 5.2). S2: QUOTED from NHMRC Centre of Research Excellence in Ear and Hearing Health of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children 'Otitis Media Guidelines — About Otitis Media' (undated web page), 3 claims; LICENCE: no licence recorded in edition 1.0; quoted with attribution, as in edition 1.0 (read at not recorded in edition 1.0). S3: QUOTED from NHMRC Centre of Research Excellence in Ear and Hearing Health of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children 'Otitis Media Guidelines — home page' (undated web page), 2 claims; LICENCE: no licence recorded in edition 1.0; quoted with attribution, as in edition 1.0 (read at not recorded in edition 1.0). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 rebuilds the Wave 1 hand-written page (edition 1.0, 2026-09-22), which quoted RCH verbatim: S1 is now a paraphrase of the RCH page re-fetched 2026-09-24, and all 29 S1 claims are carried over. S2 and S3 keep their quote mode and their Wave 1 text: their src files hold the verbatim source_text recovered from the edition 1.0 verification JSON (retrieved 2026-09-22), not a fresh fetch.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **A sick, febrile young child needs serious causes excluded** before otitis media is accepted as the only diagnosis.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **To diagnose AOM you need acute onset plus an abnormal drum** showing both middle ear inflammation and a middle ear effusion.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not give antibiotics routinely for acute otitis media.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Very common:** 75% of children have had at least one episode by the time they start school, and it peaks at 6-18 months of age.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Cigarette smoke from people in the household** is a recognised risk factor that can be changed.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Redness of the drum on its own does not mean AOM**; a viral URTI is the usual reason for it.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Normal drum:** translucent, not red, with the malleus handle upright.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Injected drum:** pink or red, commonly with fever, eustachian tube blockage or a viral URTI; still transparent because there is no effusion, and the malleus handle is clearly visible and lies more horizontally.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **AOM:** landmarks are lost, the malleus handle above all; the drum is opaque, red with inflammation or white with pus behind it.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **OME (glue ear):** the drum is pulled in and the malleus handle stands out, drawn inward and more horizontal; there may be bulging or a fluid level behind it, and a yellow or amber colour suggests fluid.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Infants, particularly under 6 months:** AOM and OME are often misdiagnosed, so give other diagnoses full consideration (see `febrile-child`).
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Management may differ for higher-risk groups**, such as children in Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander communities.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **No routine investigations for AOM.** CT or MRI is generally kept for a suspected intracranial complication.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Most childhood AOM gets better by itself**, and antibiotics are not recommended.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Pain relief is the treatment:** simple analgesia, given regularly and in adequate doses.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Severe acute ear pain, drum intact:** a short course of topical analgesia can help as an add-on, eg 1-2 drops of 2% lignocaine (the injection solution) or benzocaine + phenazone (Auralgan®). Only on an intact tympanic membrane.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Not effective in AOM:** decongestants, antihistamines, corticosteroids.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Antibiotic choice follows local susceptibility patterns and local guidelines.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Perforation is common in AOM:** the ear discharges and the pain often eases.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Tell perforation discharge apart from otitis externa.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Otitis externa:** the ear hurts when examined, and the canal skin is swollen, sometimes with thin pus.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Acute mastoiditis is rare**, yet it is the commonest suppurative complication of AOM and can come with intracranial complications.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Diagnosing mastoiditis:** inflammation behind the ear (redness, swelling, tenderness or fluctuance), an ear that sticks out, often a swollen ear canal, and signs of AOM.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Mastoiditis needs prompt IV antibiotics** (eg a 3rd generation cephalosporin) **and ENT input**, since surgery may be needed.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Facial nerve palsy from AOM: discuss with ENT.** Long-term non-suppurative sequelae include TM atelectasis and cholesteatoma.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **OME** (once called serous otitis or glue ear) is middle ear fluid with no sign or symptom of infection apart from temporary hearing loss.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **An effusion alone does not diagnose AOM**: after an episode, fluid can take up to 12 weeks to clear.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **OME usually needs neither antibiotics nor ENT referral:** most follows AOM and clears by itself, without lasting effect on language, literacy or cognitive development.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Effusion still present after 3 months:** arrange a hearing assessment and involve or refer to ENT.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, 'Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute otitis media', last updated June 2021, https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Acute_otitis_media/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Otitis media is very common in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, and near-universal in remote communities**; affected children cannot hear properly and struggle with speech, language, learning and behaviour.
claims.source_text: Many Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander children, and almost all who live in remote communities, have middle ear infection, glue ear or runny ears (otitis media, OM). Children with OM cannot hear properly and have trouble with speech, language, learning and behaviour
claims.locator: NHMRC Centre of Research Excellence in Ear and Hearing Health of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children, 'Otitis Media Guidelines — About Otitis Media', undated web page, https://otitismediaguidelines.com/about-otitis-media/, retrieved 2026-09-22

claims.claim: **Every form of otitis media causes some hearing loss**, and if it persists it can isolate a child socially, with life-long effects on communication, listening and understanding.
claims.source_text: All forms of Otitis Media cause some level of hearing loss. If hearing loss persists it can cause social isolation with life-long impacts on communication, listening and understanding
claims.locator: NHMRC Centre of Research Excellence in Ear and Hearing Health of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children, 'Otitis Media Guidelines — home page', undated web page, https://otitismediaguidelines.com/, retrieved 2026-09-22

claims.claim: **Chronic otitis media and hearing loss** make a child more vulnerable at school entry and affect attendance and performance; children with hearing loss are more likely to be maltreated.
claims.source_text: Chronic otitis media and hearing loss increases a child's vulnerability on entering school, school attendance, and performance. … Children with hearing loss are more likely to experience child maltreatment
claims.locator: NHMRC Centre of Research Excellence in Ear and Hearing Health of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children, 'Otitis Media Guidelines — home page', undated web page, https://otitismediaguidelines.com/, retrieved 2026-09-22

claims.claim: **Mechanism:** pneumococcus and non-typable *H. influenzae* (NTHi) spread from other children into the nose, then into the middle ear, where pus can burst the drum; the drum can be slow to heal and must be treated. The same nasal germs can cause pneumonia.
claims.source_text: The germs called pneumococcus (pneumo) and non-typable H. influenzae (NTHi or H'flu) get into the baby or child's nose from other children. These germs can then get inside the middle ear and cause infection and pus - like a boil - which can burst the ear drum. Unlike a boil under the skin which can heal, the eardrum can take a long time to heal and must be treated. Germs in the nose also go inside the chest to cause pneumonia
claims.locator: NHMRC Centre of Research Excellence in Ear and Hearing Health of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children, 'Otitis Media Guidelines — About Otitis Media', undated web page, https://otitismediaguidelines.com/about-otitis-media/, retrieved 2026-09-22

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Otitis media can be silent** and go unnoticed for long periods.
claims.source_text: Otitis Media may also be present without noticeable symptoms and can persist for long periods undetected
claims.locator: NHMRC Centre of Research Excellence in Ear and Hearing Health of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children, 'Otitis Media Guidelines — About Otitis Media', undated web page, https://otitismediaguidelines.com/about-otitis-media/, retrieved 2026-09-22
